claims.statement: Runtime CI requires formatting and Clippy checks, dependency audit, workspace tests, and a release build before the Docker job can run.
The Docker job can build on pull requests without publishing; qualifying pushes to main and v-prefixed tags publish to GHCR with a commit SHA tag among the generated tags.

After Docker succeeds on a push to main, CI sets Kustomize newTag to sha- plus the first seven characters of the source commit and, if changed, pushes a separate skip-CI commit. Kustomize replaces the base Deployment's main image tag with this CI-managed value.
Changes confined to k8s/ bypass runtime CI but trigger the manifest workflow on main pushes and pull requests targeting main; mixed Kubernetes and runtime changes can trigger both.
The manifest workflow runs offline Kustomize rendering and kubeconform schema validation rather than building an image or deploying to a cluster.
The runbook documents an externally owned ArgoCD Application watching main at k8s/ with no automated sync; the desired Git state can be OutOfSync until an operator manually promotes it.
The runbook provides a direct Kustomize apply for bootstrap or intentional direct deployment, and documents that the public GHCR image can be pulled without a secret.
The image builds the release proxy binary and launches it directly as UID 1000.

Kustomize generates a content-hashed ConfigMap from k8s/config.toml and rewrites the Deployment's ConfigMap volume reference so a synced config change updates the pod template; the replacement process loads the file at startup from the read-only mount identified by CONFIG_PATH.

The one-replica Recreate Deployment takes down the old pod before bringing up its replacement on a template change, causing a gap in upstream proxy availability during which tailnet clients can receive 502s.
The runbook directs operators to capture the current pod's logs before sync or restart because replacement removes access to the old pod's logs through the running Deployment.

The proxy reads OAuth credentials from /data/credentials.json on a separate ReadWriteOnce PVC; normal pod replacement and Deployment undo reuse that volume's current contents rather than reverting credentials.
On a fresh PVC without a credential file, the proxy initializes an empty credential store; an empty OAuth pool needs account enrollment before proxy traffic can be authenticated through that pool.
Pending OAuth PKCE enrollment state resides in the proxy process, so it is lost on pod replacement and is not shared across replicas.

SIGTERM starts a graceful drain of the main HTTP server with a five-second wait; on timeout the proxy logs a warning and continues shutdown, including tracer-provider shutdown when enabled. The Kubernetes pod grace period is six seconds and increasing it alone does not lengthen the application drain, so long requests or streams may not finish.

Startup, liveness, and readiness probes all use HTTP /health on the proxy's port 8080. Startup gates the other probes; liveness failures can trigger restarts and readiness failures remove the pod from Service traffic.

The health route bypasses the proxy concurrency limiter and returns HTTP 200 with provider status and optional pool details in JSON even when the OAuth pool reports unhealthy; HTTP probe success is not proof that a real authenticated request will work.

ArgoCD Healthy does not establish that the intended Git revision was synced; promotion verification checks the operation result and revision, then the Deployment rollout and replacement pod rather than treating the template's intended image as a running container.

The tailnet HTTPS request path uses the Tailscale Ingress and the proxy ClusterIP Service on port 80 targeting container port 8080; the admin ClusterIP Service on port 9090 is separate and not exercised by that path.

The operator-side live:validate task compares origin/main's Kustomize tag with the Deployment template image and reports the last ArgoCD sync revision and time; tag drift warns without failing the task by itself.

Live validation uses cluster and tailnet access to inspect deployed objects, check HTTP health, execute a Pi smoke request, and check for recent OAuth proxy spans in Phoenix; these are not verified by offline CI.

Focused offline tests cover health and metrics responsiveness when the proxy concurrency slot is occupied and credential persistence across a disk reload; they do not provision a Kubernetes PVC or exercise the deployed tailnet path.

A durable rollback reverts the offending Git change and manually syncs the corrected desired state; a code revert gets a newly built and pinned image, whereas a change confined to Kubernetes manifests takes the manifest validation path without an image rebuild.

Emergency Kubernetes rollout undo restores an available Deployment pod template, not Git or separately managed resources. A previous generated ConfigMap must still exist if that template references it, and a later manual sync can overwrite the undo with the desired state in main.

Rolling back or restarting the proxy does not repair an expired OAuth credential stored on the persistent volume; pool failures caused by rejected refresh grants require account recovery rather than pod replacement.
